approach.method_basis: The Parent first trains a recurrent SMILES language model on an unlabeled molecular corpus. Each objective starts with a fresh policy copied from that prior, which then stays frozen. After each accepted batch, the policy fits the best-scoring half of the current molecules and a uniformly sampled group of earlier elites. Every target is the frozen prior log probability of the molecule's original accepted SMILES plus sixty times its real score, with equal weight for each training sequence. A memory keeps the thirty-two highest-scoring previously selected elites, preserving their original strings and scores. The updated policy directly samples complete SMILES, and chemical validation and canonical duplicate rejection fill the next batch.
approach.novelty: Replace uniform historical sampling with score-ordered replay: use the highest-scoring eligible historical molecules, keeping the same replay count. This makes the best accepted evidence already present in memory determine the historical training group. It leaves admission, retention and the learning rule intact. Earlier siblings explored the prior representation and training; the original replay experiment established that using history changes learning, but did not test whether preferentially selecting stronger history helps. A passive uniform draw on the same memory and a comparison of the two gradients will show whether this selection changes the evidence actually fitted. Concentration and useful novel molecules remain separate outcomes, because repeatedly choosing strong examples can also narrow exploration.

hypothesis: Replace uniform historical-elite replay membership with the highest accepted-score eligible records, ordered by descending score and canonical identity, while preserving the inherited replay count, original accepted sequence and reward provenance, memory admission/retention and equal-per-sequence online learning.

finding_summary.headline: Stronger historical replay changed learning, narrowed exploration and gave uneven score gains.
finding_summary.insights:
The experiment separates using replay from choosing its members. Historical replay already supplied measurable gradients in the Parent; selecting the strongest available history demonstrably changed both the reward distribution and the gradient of the loss actually optimized. The comparison uses the child's own memory and policy state, so it establishes the selection effect without inventing an alternative scored trajectory. Stronger reward did not mean a larger gradient: on changed updates, the mean actual combined-gradient norm was about 363 versus 493 for the passive uniform group. Repeatedly selected records were often already closer to their targets, and historical mean squared error moved only from 105.05 to 102.64 across the real updates; 834 of 2,100 historical row exposures nevertheless worsened.

The tradeoff is a narrower stream of accepted evidence and more repeated proposals. That concentration is visible in chemistry as well: the deco-hop proposal set fell from 529 to 392 distinct cores and the strongest neighborhoods repeatedly decorate related aromatic, amide, urea, amine or hydrazone families. Conventional connectivity remains dominant, but score ordering alone does not improve attachment chemistry, control oversized outliers or add missing stereochemical configurations. Positive augmented targets also persist in 595 of 2,100 historical exposures, despite being above the log-probability ceiling. The campaign now has evidence that reward enrichment can improve some endpoints while reducing novelty and producing inconsistent gains; preserving a broader supply of useful accepted evidence is an open question separate from whether this selector activates.
finding_summary.results:
The selection mechanism ran on the intended records. All 405 nonterminal updates with surplus eligible history changed replay membership and increased accepted replay reward relative to the passive uniform draw on that same memory. Across all 420 nonterminal historical updates, replay reward rose from the uniform comparator's 0.301506 to 0.376503; the fifteen no-surplus updates had no reward difference. Selected history exceeded the current elite mean in 370 updates, compared with 185 for the uniform comparator. All 405 changed selections also produced measurable changes in the actual training gradient at the registered tolerance. Original accepted strings, scores, chronological admission, top-32 retention, equal row weights and frozen priors were preserved.

The stronger replay was more concentrated: summing distinct replayed identities within the fifteen objective sessions gave 540 actual identities versus 1,103 under the passive comparator, and 335 versus 751 distinct Murcko cores. Actual replay was younger on average, at 4.47 batches versus 5.52, rather than simply older. In subsequent generation, raw validity increased from Parent 90.43% to 92.58%, while duplicate draws rose from 30.11% to 40.78% and novel yield fell from 60.31% to 51.81%. Forty-one batches needed additional sampling, versus five in the Parent. All fifteen tasks still completed the same 300-call budgets.

Mean final Top-1 increased from 0.507554 to 0.513272, a paired mean gain of 0.005718. The three paired changes were -0.012216, +0.009216 and +0.020155, so the benefit was uneven across replicas. Four task means increased; sitagliptin decreased. The final fifteen updates are excluded from the selection-to-proposal conclusions because no later proposals follow them.

molecular.headline: Conventional aromatic medicinal chemistry spans many cores, with concentrated high-score families and no assigned stereochemistry
molecular.overall_character: The supplied trajectories cover all five objectives and all three seeds: each task contains 900 evaluated molecules, including 870 optimizer proposals. All 4,350 optimizer-proposal SMILES parse with RDKit. This is predominantly recognizable medicinal chemistry: aromatic and heteroaromatic rings linked through amides, ureas, hydrazones, amines and sulfonamides. Proposal median heavy-atom counts are 24, 30, 28, 23 and 24 in the supplied task order; median ring counts are three throughout. Digest aromatic-token rates are 0.9586-0.9908 and ring-closure rates 0.9782-0.9977, so lack of rings or aromaticity is not the central deficit. Across individual tasks, 392-737 distinct nonchiral Murcko scaffolds occur among proposals, although the digest leaders repeatedly occupy close analogue families. Dominant structures have plausible conventional connectivity; occasional azides, peroxides, haloalkyl chains and very large products warrant separate scrutiny. These trajectories do not establish synthesis, stability, solubility or experimental activity. Relative to the parent, aromatic medicinal chemistry remains central, while the leading families change: pyrazole carboxamides and pyrrolylmethyl ureas replace prominent indole amides, flexible diamines join the strongest amine chemotypes, and acylhydrazones are more prominent in one otherwise weak-score session. No assigned stereocentres occur in optimizer proposals; molecules with unassigned stereocentres number 107, 76, 338, 201 and 286 in task order. Ring-rich generation therefore coexists with incomplete stereochemical specification.

per_task.generated_character: Proposals usually have a compact aromatic framework: median 24 heavy atoms and three aromatic rings. The leading approximately 0.470 family consists of N-aryl pyrazole carboxamides bearing an N-(1-arylethyl) amide substituent; the approximately 0.468 family comprises an N-methylpyrrolylmethyl group attached to a diaryl urea. Both are conventional three-ring medicinal-chemistry structures with carbonyl hydrogen-bonding groups and substantial aryl halogenation. An aza-fused aromatic hydroxy carboxamide also appears among the digest leaders. This differs from the parent leaders, which included substituted indole carboxamides. The low end includes long-chain ester elaboration and much larger, multiply linked ring systems, rather than an absence of valid or aromatic structures.
liabilities: Repeated aryl bromine and chlorine substitution can increase molecular mass without demonstrating a score benefit in the cited equal-score families.
Long alkyl tails and elaborate linked frameworks produce severe low-score outliers despite chemically recognizable bonding.
missing_features: Systematic exploration of alternative compact aromatic/carbonyl arrangements is underrepresented among the leading examples relative to repeated halogen variants; no specific unobserved target scaffold can be inferred.
The leading arylethyl carboxamides contain an unassigned stereogenic carbon, so the generated molecules do not specify which three-dimensional configuration is being proposed.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The supplied leaders associate moderate molecular size and organized aromatic/carbonyl substitution with scores near 0.47. Scores are identical within several halogen substitutions and positional variants, so these examples do not establish a reward for further halo decoration. Extending an indole ester with a very long alkyl chain gives about 3.14e-24, while an elaborate ring-and-linker-rich amide reaches about 9.07e-27. Those comparisons support size and arrangement sensitivity, but are not matched transformations isolating a single cause. Final pyrrolylmethyl urea analogues score about 0.423-0.436, showing that related heteroaromatic substitutions can retain appreciable score without reaching the listed maximum.

per_task.generated_character: This is the largest and most halogen-rich typical proposal set: median 30 heavy atoms, median molecular mass 437.343 and digest halogen rate 0.8701. The leading molecules have three aromatic six-membered rings, heavily fluorinated aryl groups, a substituted pyridine core, and aminomethyl, benzylamine or amide connections. A separate leading family contains diarylamino acylhydrazones. These are plausible synthetic motifs, although their dense fluorination and largely aromatic frameworks create substantial mass and polarity-distribution questions. Full trajectories contain 187 proposals matching an N-N=C connection. Compared with the parent, fluorinated aromatic and hydrazone chemistry persists, with the current leaders including less fused, three-ring pyridyl amine and amide architectures.
liabilities: Dense aryl fluorination and mostly aromatic frameworks can produce high molecular mass and limited three-dimensional shape; the trajectories contain no physical-property measurements.
Acylhydrazones and thiourea/imine variants introduce geometry, tautomerism and stability questions that a valid SMILES string does not settle.
Nine optimizer proposals exceed 50 heavy atoms; extending size is not itself supported as the useful structural feature.
missing_features: The leading repertoire supplies many fluorinated aromatic analogues but less evidence for chemically different architectures retaining the same useful spatial and electronic arrangement.
Hydrazone and imine examples do not specify C=N geometry; their displayed scores do not identify which configurational or tautomeric form would carry the implied interactions.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The top aminomethyl pyridyl structure scores 0.603953 and related amines or amides lie close to 0.60. A useful local contrast is the methylthio pyridyl amide at 0.599304 versus its methylsulfonyl counterpart at 0.343569: the rest of their displayed framework is the same, supporting sensitivity to sulfur oxidation state in that chemical context. It does not establish that sulfones are generally unfavorable. The small cyanophenyl sulfone scores 0.257003, whereas terminal aromatic thiourea/imine structures reach approximately 0.57-0.59. Size alone therefore does not explain the full gradient.

per_task.generated_character: The strongest displayed chemistry includes very flexible acyclic diamines: a tertiary nitrogen connects an N-butyl group, an arylbutyl group and a propyl secondary-benzylamine arm. Those molecules carry two halogenated aromatic rings and no saturated nitrogen ring. Another high-scoring family combines an arylpiperidine with an aminoethyl arylamine substituent. These are recognizable amine-rich medicinal-chemistry structures, with median proposal heavy-atom count 28 and median fraction of sp3 carbons about 0.529. Parent leaders instead prominently included arylpiperazine/indole combinations and fused aryl amines, so useful amine-plus-aromatic chemistry spans several topologies. Low-score examples are often amide-, sulfonamide- or acylhydrazone-rich aromatic structures with fewer clearly basic aliphatic amine sites.
liabilities: Long alkyl linkers, N-butyl or N-pentyl groups and heavy aryl halogens create substantial conformational freedom and mass; the leading chlorobromo diamine has molecular mass 465.907.
Several cited terminal molecules carry primary bromoalkyl or iodoalkyl groups, introducing possible electrophilic side-chain liabilities that the objective values do not characterize.
Ten proposals exceed 50 heavy atoms and the largest reaches 81, so the proposal distribution includes much larger structures than the leading compact ring/amine frameworks.
missing_features: No additional functional group can be inferred as necessary from near-ceiling scores; broader economical coverage of the observed amine/aromatic arrangements is the supported chemical coverage gap.
Three-dimensional specification remains incomplete across the full proposal set: 338 proposals contain an unassigned stereocentre, although the leading flexible diamine itself is achiral.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The flexible diamines reach 0.999998 and the arylpiperidine example 0.999994. Both retain accessible amine functionality and separated aromatic regions, supporting those shared features as a chemical association in this trajectory; a saturated nitrogen ring is not required by the leading examples. A compact nitro/acid heteroaromatic amide is near 1.86e-05 and a sulfonamide-substituted heteroaryl amide near 1.98e-05. In the final molecules, a tertiary amine with two bromobutyl arms and no aromatic ring scores 0.123770, while more extended molecules retaining a benzylamine-bearing aryl region score around 0.90 or above. These are contextual associations rather than measured binding or isolated substituent effects.

per_task.generated_character: Median proposals contain 23 heavy atoms and three rings, with 729 distinct nonchiral Murcko scaffolds among optimizer proposals. The leading family is arylsulfonylpiperazine chemistry: examples attach sulfonyl phenylpiperazine to a fused aza-lactam or chromanone-like framework, or attach N-methylpiperazine sulfonamide to substituted biphenyl systems. Those molecules combine aromatic surfaces, a saturated six-membered nitrogen ring, sulfonyl oxygens and sometimes an additional carbonyl. The parent also produced a leading N-methyl arylsulfonylpiperazine, alongside fused lactam and diaryl heterocyclic alternatives. The current leading structures are generally plausible synthetic chemotypes; the very low end includes carbon disulfide, allyl azide and small unusual or highly polar fragments.
liabilities: Small disconnected-from-the-leading-chemotype proposals include carbon disulfide and an organic azide, yielding little useful structural overlap with the higher-scoring multi-ring molecules.
Sulfonylation changes the electronic character of a ring nitrogen; counting every nitrogen as an interchangeable basic amine would misdescribe this family.
Some terminal proposals add multiple sulfur/nitrogen connections and tautomeric heterocycles without demonstrating improved placement of the leading polar groups.
missing_features: The output covers many core identities but supplies limited evidence for precise alternative placements of its useful aromatic, sulfonyl and amine regions beyond the leading analogue neighborhood.
Leading alternatives include an unspecified stereocentre in the chromanone-like example, and 201 proposals have an unassigned stereocentre; configurationally explicit versions are absent.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The fused aza-lactam sulfonylphenylpiperazine reaches 0.235468, a chromanone-like analogue 0.229568 and a methoxy biphenyl N-methylsulfonylpiperazine 0.222204. These support a combined multi-ring and polar-linker architecture in the observed neighborhood. Carbon disulfide and allyl azide score zero, while a heavily hydroxylated cyclic acid scores 0.013472: fragmentation or abundant oxygen alone does not reproduce the arrangement in the leaders. Other aromatic, carbonyl-containing terminal molecules remain near 0.10-0.15. The molecular evidence does not identify a single missing substituent capable of resolving the remaining low scores.

per_task.generated_character: The highest molecule is a compact N-methylbenzamide attached to a substituted fused azaheteroaromatic system bearing a hydroxyl group; it has 22 heavy atoms and three aromatic rings. Other leaders are substituted anisyl/pyridyl acylhydrazones, generally with two aromatic rings, and an aryl hydroxyethyl carboxamide attached to a pyrazole. These are recognizable, synthetically plausible chemical families rather than unusual-valence graphs. Full proposals have median 24 heavy atoms, three rings and 737 distinct nonchiral Murcko scaffolds. Relative to the parent leaders, which included sulfonamide/acyl heterocycles and fused imino carbonyl systems, the current digest is particularly concentrated in pyridyl acylhydrazones; N-N=C matches increase from 71 to 116 proposals. Worst examples include extremely large polycyclic, macrocyclic peptide-like or long-chain aromatic elaborations.
liabilities: Acylhydrazone enrichment brings possible E/Z, tautomeric and stability concerns that are not resolved by the objective scores.
Large aromatic appendages, long alkyl chains and oversized cyclic structures coincide with vanishing scores; six proposals exceed 50 heavy atoms.
The proposal set contains 286 molecules with an unassigned stereocentre and no assigned stereocentres, limiting interpretation of any geometry-dependent chemistry.
missing_features: Broader coverage of compact, correctly arranged polar heteroaromatic/carbonyl chemotypes is missing from the higher-score repertoire, which repeatedly returns close acylhydrazone analogues despite many proposed scaffolds.
The hydroxyethyl amide leader has an unassigned stereogenic alcohol carbon, while hydrazone leaders do not specify C=N geometry; these structures do not establish stereochemical adequacy.

The evidence supports no unique mandatory target-like group: the best displayed molecule is distinct from the repeated hydrazone family, so extrapolation should preserve access to alternative compact cores.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The compact benzamide/azaheteroaromatic structure scores 0.309504, the acetyl-substituted anisyl pyridyl acylhydrazone 0.281351, and the hydroxyethyl pyrazole carboxamide 0.274759. A dimethoxy aryl pyridyl acylhydrazone scores 0.233893, whereas the corresponding displayed acetyl hydrazone with the heteroaryl acyl region replaced scores 0.002010. Enlarging a methoxy substituent to a benzyl/CF3-bearing arm gives approximately 1.33e-09 despite retaining a pyridyl acylhydrazone. Thus functional-group placement and controlled size both appear relevant within the visible examples. The digest median is rounded to 0.0: the full 900-row trajectory median is approximately 3.19e-07 and only two rows are exactly zero. The displayed higher-score chemotypes occupy a sparse part of a mostly very low-score distribution.

transferable_gaps.evidence: A displayed pyridyl amide scores 0.599304 with a methylthio substituent and 0.343569 with the corresponding methylsulfonyl group. In another supplied session, a pyridyl acylhydrazone scores 0.233893 while the displayed acetyl hydrazone counterpart scores 0.002010. High-scoring amine-rich structures also differ chemically from lower-scoring amide and sulfonamide nitrogen environments. These examples show that heteroatom counts alone do not explain the observed gradient.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator covers many atoms and functional groups but does not consistently preserve their useful attachment and electronic context.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Preserve access to chemically valid attachment-point and oxidation-state alternatives, and learn their value from observed feedback in their local structural context. Treat amines, amide nitrogens, sulfonamide nitrogens, thioethers and sulfones as different chemical environments rather than interchangeable token decorations.

transferable_gaps.evidence: Individual proposal sets contain 392-737 distinct nonchiral Murcko scaffolds, yet digest leaders cluster into pyrazole carboxamides, pyrrolylmethyl ureas, polyfluorinated pyridyl structures, flexible diamines, arylsulfonylpiperazines and acylhydrazones. Several halo-substitution or positional variants have identical displayed scores. Another session contains 737 scaffold identities while its full-trajectory median score is approximately 3.19e-07, showing that identity breadth is not sufficient chemical coverage of useful regions.
transferable_gaps.gap: Broad scaffold counts coexist with narrow high-score analogue families and repeated peripheral halogen variation.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Support core and linker alternatives that preserve chemically meaningful arrangements already associated with reward, alongside local substitution. Assess useful chemical coverage from observed structural neighborhoods and feedback, without assuming that more unique strings or more halogen substitutions alone expands the productive repertoire.

transferable_gaps.evidence: No assigned stereocentres occur in the 4,350 optimizer proposals; the five sessions contain 107, 76, 338, 201 and 286 proposals with at least one unassigned stereocentre. Digest leaders include an arylethyl carboxamide, a chromanone-like ring and a benzylic alcohol whose stereocentres are unspecified. Acylhydrazone leaders also omit explicit C=N geometry. The leading flexible diamine is achiral, so stereochemical specification is a conditional need rather than a universal requirement.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator leaves stereogenic structures and configurationally ambiguous imine chemistry unspecified.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Represent and sample stereochemistry where a generated structure actually supports it, retaining chemically consistent configurations and bond geometry. Let feedback determine the usefulness of these alternatives, and keep achiral and configurationally explicit structures accessible without assuming an unobserved preferred stereoisomer.

transferable_gaps.evidence: Proposal median heavy-atom counts are 24, 30, 28, 23 and 24, but the numbers exceeding 50 heavy atoms are 1, 9, 10, 0 and 6. Cited low-score molecules include very long alkyl esters and oversized aromatic or macrocyclic structures. In a close hydrazone neighborhood, replacing a compact methoxy substituent with a benzyl/CF3-bearing extension accompanies a score near 1.33e-09. Conversely, flexible multi-amine chains can score near the ceiling, while some related proposals introduce primary bromoalkyl or iodoalkyl groups.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator lacks consistent context-sensitive control of molecular growth, flexible side chains and reactive appendages.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Maintain alternatives with controlled linker length, appendage size and functional-group reactivity, using local feedback to distinguish useful flexibility from destructive growth. A single global preference for small, rigid or ring-bound structures would discard demonstrated useful chemistry; the needed capability is contextual structural control and chemically informed handling of side-chain motifs.

method_name: Augmented Hill-Climb with a corpus-trained SMILES policy
method_thesis: Train a compact autoregressive SMILES prior solely on the supplied unlabeled corpus, then initialize a fresh policy from that prior for each objective. Use the initial observations and each subsequent scored batch to update only its highest-reward sequences with the Augmented Hill-Climb loss: fit policy log likelihood to frozen-prior log likelihood plus scaled observed reward. Sample complete molecules token by token from the updated policy, canonicalize them, and refill invalid or duplicate proposals by further generation. The corpus supplies language training, never a ranked molecular pool. Elite-conditioned policy updates should shift generation toward new high-scoring molecular combinations quickly enough to improve the benchmark's mean final Top-1. This is a small-budget transfer hypothesis, not a claim that published larger-budget gains carry over. The root uses the current scored batch; randomized historical replay is reserved for the first improvement. The anchor's elite augmented-likelihood mechanism is described by [Thomas et al.](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-022-00646-z).

activation_observables.measurement: For each nonterminal update, reconstruct actual top-score replay and the passive inherited uniform indices on the identical eligible memory. Confirm the passive session NumPy draw stream and comparator members, and count actual/comparator identity-set differences. Conditional on the uniform draw omitting stronger eligible records, actual replay mean accepted reward must exceed the comparator; it must never be smaller beyond 1e-12. Register a positive pooled actual-minus-comparator reward difference over nonterminal selection-opportunity updates. activation_observables.measurement: Keep inherited finite-tolerance historical-only and actual combined-minus-current gradient diagnostics at pre-update parameters and fixed targets. Additionally compare actual score-ordered combined gradients with passive uniform combined gradients evaluated at those same parameters, preserving equal per-sequence loss weights. applicability_conditions: The direct evidence is a same-memory read-only counterfactual on the complete three-seed Parent; its reward improvements are not predicted scores for unevaluated molecules or independent counterfactual training trajectories.

Only earlier accepted selected elites from this objective may supply replay. All current-batch identities remain excluded and the existing exact accepted records, memory capacity and admission timing remain unchanged.

The mechanism can change membership only with more eligible history than replay positions. Strict reward enrichment requires unequal accepted rewards and a uniform comparator omitting stronger records; tied/no-surplus cases must be reported separately.

Selecting higher scores can repeatedly emphasize a narrow family and can increase the frequency of inherited positive augmented-log-probability targets. No weighting, target correction, diversity penalty, view augmentation or proposal edit is part of this experiment.

Novel chemical transfer and final-best score benefit remain empirical. The Parent chemistry gaps in attachment arrangements, size control, reactive outliers and stereochemistry are not solved by selecting high scores alone.

The historical replay cluster already demonstrates accepted-history activation. This child changes its selection mechanism on the replicated replay Parent; the current-only root and the four prior-training siblings do not settle that conditional question.

research_intent.falsifier: The selection mechanism is refuted if eligible actual training members do not equal the highest accepted-score chronological records with the inherited count and tie rule, if accepted provenance or retention changes, or if there is no positive actual-minus-uniform replay reward movement despite observed opportunities to replace weaker records. finding_summary.headline: Stronger historical replay changed learning, narrowed exploration and gave uneven score gains.
finding_summary.insights:
The experiment separates using replay from choosing its members. Historical replay already supplied measurable gradients in the Parent; selecting the strongest available history demonstrably changed both the reward distribution and the gradient of the loss actually optimized. The comparison uses the child's own memory and policy state, so it establishes the selection effect without inventing an alternative scored trajectory. Stronger reward did not mean a larger gradient: on changed updates, the mean actual combined-gradient norm was about 363 versus 493 for the passive uniform group. Repeatedly selected records were often already closer to their targets, and historical mean squared error moved only from 105.05 to 102.64 across the real updates; 834 of 2,100 historical row exposures nevertheless worsened.

The tradeoff is a narrower stream of accepted evidence and more repeated proposals. That concentration is visible in chemistry as well: the deco-hop proposal set fell from 529 to 392 distinct cores and the strongest neighborhoods repeatedly decorate related aromatic, amide, urea, amine or hydrazone families. Conventional connectivity remains dominant, but score ordering alone does not improve attachment chemistry, control oversized outliers or add missing stereochemical configurations. Positive augmented targets also persist in 595 of 2,100 historical exposures, despite being above the log-probability ceiling. The campaign now has evidence that reward enrichment can improve some endpoints while reducing novelty and producing inconsistent gains; preserving a broader supply of useful accepted evidence is an open question separate from whether this selector activates.
finding_summary.results:
The selection mechanism ran on the intended records. All 405 nonterminal updates with surplus eligible history changed replay membership and increased accepted replay reward relative to the passive uniform draw on that same memory. Across all 420 nonterminal historical updates, replay reward rose from the uniform comparator's 0.301506 to 0.376503; the fifteen no-surplus updates had no reward difference. Selected history exceeded the current elite mean in 370 updates, compared with 185 for the uniform comparator. All 405 changed selections also produced measurable changes in the actual training gradient at the registered tolerance. Original accepted strings, scores, chronological admission, top-32 retention, equal row weights and frozen priors were preserved.

The stronger replay was more concentrated: summing distinct replayed identities within the fifteen objective sessions gave 540 actual identities versus 1,103 under the passive comparator, and 335 versus 751 distinct Murcko cores. Actual replay was younger on average, at 4.47 batches versus 5.52, rather than simply older. In subsequent generation, raw validity increased from Parent 90.43% to 92.58%, while duplicate draws rose from 30.11% to 40.78% and novel yield fell from 60.31% to 51.81%. Forty-one batches needed additional sampling, versus five in the Parent. All fifteen tasks still completed the same 300-call budgets.

Mean final Top-1 increased from 0.507554 to 0.513272, a paired mean gain of 0.005718. The three paired changes were -0.012216, +0.009216 and +0.020155, so the benefit was uneven across replicas. Four task means increased; sitagliptin decreased. The final fifteen updates are excluded from the selection-to-proposal conclusions because no later proposals follow them.

observable_measurements.name: Compare proposed retention or replay selection with the inherited rule on the same eligible memory; measure changed training identities, age and reward distributions, core coverage, and stronger-history opportunities.

At fixed pre-update parameters and accepted targets, measure historical-only gradients and the actual combined-minus-current gradient, with explicit finite tolerances and no diagnostic optimizer steps; distinguish logged membership from actual loss contribution.

possible_failure_causes: No provenance, retention, selection, gradient-contribution or execution falsifier triggered. All 405 nonterminal changed selections enriched replay reward and changed gradients, and all fifteen task replicas completed.

Selecting the strongest history reduced the number of distinct replayed identities and cores, increased repeated raw proposals and required more refill sampling. This is observed concentration cost, even though every final submitted batch remained valid and novel.

Historical records can already be near their targets. Stronger rewards therefore do not imply larger useful gradients: actual combined gradients are smaller on average than the same-state uniform comparator, and real updates worsen 834 of 2,100 individual historical target errors while improving the pooled mean.

The inherited prior-log-probability plus 60*score rule produces positive unattainable historical targets in 595 exposures, versus 541 in Parent nonterminal history. They remain uncorrected by design and can maintain pressure toward repeated favored sequences.
Macro gains are mixed across seeds and task effects vary. The positive mean is not evidence of a uniformly better endpoint or of broader chemically useful transfer.

Full intermediate policy tensors and gradient vectors were not retained, so independent analysis validates scalar gradient receipts and their exact accepted inputs rather than replaying all optimization. The unchanged optimizer source and recorded actual updates support contribution without an additional training experiment.

applicability_conditions: Supported on the complete three-seed direct-policy Parent with the identical prepared priors, current top-half elites, historical replay count and top-32 accepted memory. Only earlier selected elites from the current objective are eligible, and current-batch identities are excluded.

Strict reward and gradient activation is established on 405 nonterminal surplus opportunities. Fifteen no-surplus historical updates cannot change membership; none changes reward or exceeds the selection-gradient tolerance. No score-tied historical eligible memory or empty accepted batch occurred.

The same-memory uniform comparator consumes exactly the inherited session NumPy draw but does not train, alter memory or receive a new oracle label. Its selection metrics and gradients are not counterfactual trajectory scores.

Both actual and comparator losses preserve equal per-sequence weight and exact frozen-prior plus accepted-score targets. Diagnostic optimizer-step counts are zero, and the real optimizer trains actual selected history with the original clipping, learning rate and step cap.
All chronology and frozen-prior checks cover terminal updates, but the fifteen terminal updates are separately reported and cannot explain any later sampled molecule.

Useful novelty and chemistry must be measured independently of replay reward or parseable output. The generated molecules remain largely conventional aromatic medicinal chemistry with concentrated families, occasional liabilities and no assigned stereochemistry.
The observed score effect is complete but uneven across the three seeds. No new candidate, model training, optimizer update or oracle evaluation was run during analysis.

finding_summary.headline: Stronger historical replay changed learning, narrowed exploration and gave uneven score gains.
finding_summary.insights:
The experiment separates using replay from choosing its members. Historical replay already supplied measurable gradients in the Parent; selecting the strongest available history demonstrably changed both the reward distribution and the gradient of the loss actually optimized. The comparison uses the child's own memory and policy state, so it establishes the selection effect without inventing an alternative scored trajectory. Stronger reward did not mean a larger gradient: on changed updates, the mean actual combined-gradient norm was about 363 versus 493 for the passive uniform group. Repeatedly selected records were often already closer to their targets, and historical mean squared error moved only from 105.05 to 102.64 across the real updates; 834 of 2,100 historical row exposures nevertheless worsened.

The tradeoff is a narrower stream of accepted evidence and more repeated proposals. That concentration is visible in chemistry as well: the deco-hop proposal set fell from 529 to 392 distinct cores and the strongest neighborhoods repeatedly decorate related aromatic, amide, urea, amine or hydrazone families. Conventional connectivity remains dominant, but score ordering alone does not improve attachment chemistry, control oversized outliers or add missing stereochemical configurations. Positive augmented targets also persist in 595 of 2,100 historical exposures, despite being above the log-probability ceiling. The campaign now has evidence that reward enrichment can improve some endpoints while reducing novelty and producing inconsistent gains; preserving a broader supply of useful accepted evidence is an open question separate from whether this selector activates.
finding_summary.results:
The selection mechanism ran on the intended records. All 405 nonterminal updates with surplus eligible history changed replay membership and increased accepted replay reward relative to the passive uniform draw on that same memory. Across all 420 nonterminal historical updates, replay reward rose from the uniform comparator's 0.301506 to 0.376503; the fifteen no-surplus updates had no reward difference. Selected history exceeded the current elite mean in 370 updates, compared with 185 for the uniform comparator. All 405 changed selections also produced measurable changes in the actual training gradient at the registered tolerance. Original accepted strings, scores, chronological admission, top-32 retention, equal row weights and frozen priors were preserved.

The stronger replay was more concentrated: summing distinct replayed identities within the fifteen objective sessions gave 540 actual identities versus 1,103 under the passive comparator, and 335 versus 751 distinct Murcko cores. Actual replay was younger on average, at 4.47 batches versus 5.52, rather than simply older. In subsequent generation, raw validity increased from Parent 90.43% to 92.58%, while duplicate draws rose from 30.11% to 40.78% and novel yield fell from 60.31% to 51.81%. Forty-one batches needed additional sampling, versus five in the Parent. All fifteen tasks still completed the same 300-call budgets.

Mean final Top-1 increased from 0.507554 to 0.513272, a paired mean gain of 0.005718. The three paired changes were -0.012216, +0.009216 and +0.020155, so the benefit was uneven across replicas. Four task means increased; sitagliptin decreased. The final fifteen updates are excluded from the selection-to-proposal conclusions because no later proposals follow them.

observable_measurements.name: Compare proposed retention or replay selection with the inherited rule on the same eligible memory; measure changed training identities, age and reward distributions, core coverage, and stronger-history opportunities.

At fixed pre-update parameters and accepted targets, measure historical-only gradients and the actual combined-minus-current gradient, with explicit finite tolerances and no diagnostic optimizer steps; distinguish logged membership from actual loss contribution.

possible_failure_causes: No provenance, retention, selection, gradient-contribution or execution falsifier triggered. All 405 nonterminal changed selections enriched replay reward and changed gradients, and all fifteen task replicas completed.

Selecting the strongest history reduced the number of distinct replayed identities and cores, increased repeated raw proposals and required more refill sampling. This is observed concentration cost, even though every final submitted batch remained valid and novel.

Historical records can already be near their targets. Stronger rewards therefore do not imply larger useful gradients: actual combined gradients are smaller on average than the same-state uniform comparator, and real updates worsen 834 of 2,100 individual historical target errors while improving the pooled mean.

The inherited prior-log-probability plus 60*score rule produces positive unattainable historical targets in 595 exposures, versus 541 in Parent nonterminal history. They remain uncorrected by design and can maintain pressure toward repeated favored sequences.
Macro gains are mixed across seeds and task effects vary. The positive mean is not evidence of a uniformly better endpoint or of broader chemically useful transfer.

Full intermediate policy tensors and gradient vectors were not retained, so independent analysis validates scalar gradient receipts and their exact accepted inputs rather than replaying all optimization. The unchanged optimizer source and recorded actual updates support contribution without an additional training experiment.

applicability_conditions: Supported on the complete three-seed direct-policy Parent with the identical prepared priors, current top-half elites, historical replay count and top-32 accepted memory. Only earlier selected elites from the current objective are eligible, and current-batch identities are excluded.

Strict reward and gradient activation is established on 405 nonterminal surplus opportunities. Fifteen no-surplus historical updates cannot change membership; none changes reward or exceeds the selection-gradient tolerance. No score-tied historical eligible memory or empty accepted batch occurred.

The same-memory uniform comparator consumes exactly the inherited session NumPy draw but does not train, alter memory or receive a new oracle label. Its selection metrics and gradients are not counterfactual trajectory scores.

Both actual and comparator losses preserve equal per-sequence weight and exact frozen-prior plus accepted-score targets. Diagnostic optimizer-step counts are zero, and the real optimizer trains actual selected history with the original clipping, learning rate and step cap.
All chronology and frozen-prior checks cover terminal updates, but the fifteen terminal updates are separately reported and cannot explain any later sampled molecule.

Useful novelty and chemistry must be measured independently of replay reward or parseable output. The generated molecules remain largely conventional aromatic medicinal chemistry with concentrated families, occasional liabilities and no assigned stereochemistry.
The observed score effect is complete but uneven across the three seeds. No new candidate, model training, optimizer update or oracle evaluation was run during analysis.

finding_summary.headline: Stronger historical replay changed learning, narrowed exploration and gave uneven score gains.
finding_summary.insights:
The experiment separates using replay from choosing its members. Historical replay already supplied measurable gradients in the Parent; selecting the strongest available history demonstrably changed both the reward distribution and the gradient of the loss actually optimized. The comparison uses the child's own memory and policy state, so it establishes the selection effect without inventing an alternative scored trajectory. Stronger reward did not mean a larger gradient: on changed updates, the mean actual combined-gradient norm was about 363 versus 493 for the passive uniform group. Repeatedly selected records were often already closer to their targets, and historical mean squared error moved only from 105.05 to 102.64 across the real updates; 834 of 2,100 historical row exposures nevertheless worsened.

The tradeoff is a narrower stream of accepted evidence and more repeated proposals. That concentration is visible in chemistry as well: the deco-hop proposal set fell from 529 to 392 distinct cores and the strongest neighborhoods repeatedly decorate related aromatic, amide, urea, amine or hydrazone families. Conventional connectivity remains dominant, but score ordering alone does not improve attachment chemistry, control oversized outliers or add missing stereochemical configurations. Positive augmented targets also persist in 595 of 2,100 historical exposures, despite being above the log-probability ceiling. The campaign now has evidence that reward enrichment can improve some endpoints while reducing novelty and producing inconsistent gains; preserving a broader supply of useful accepted evidence is an open question separate from whether this selector activates.
finding_summary.results:
The selection mechanism ran on the intended records. All 405 nonterminal updates with surplus eligible history changed replay membership and increased accepted replay reward relative to the passive uniform draw on that same memory. Across all 420 nonterminal historical updates, replay reward rose from the uniform comparator's 0.301506 to 0.376503; the fifteen no-surplus updates had no reward difference. Selected history exceeded the current elite mean in 370 updates, compared with 185 for the uniform comparator. All 405 changed selections also produced measurable changes in the actual training gradient at the registered tolerance. Original accepted strings, scores, chronological admission, top-32 retention, equal row weights and frozen priors were preserved.

The stronger replay was more concentrated: summing distinct replayed identities within the fifteen objective sessions gave 540 actual identities versus 1,103 under the passive comparator, and 335 versus 751 distinct Murcko cores. Actual replay was younger on average, at 4.47 batches versus 5.52, rather than simply older. In subsequent generation, raw validity increased from Parent 90.43% to 92.58%, while duplicate draws rose from 30.11% to 40.78% and novel yield fell from 60.31% to 51.81%. Forty-one batches needed additional sampling, versus five in the Parent. All fifteen tasks still completed the same 300-call budgets.

Mean final Top-1 increased from 0.507554 to 0.513272, a paired mean gain of 0.005718. The three paired changes were -0.012216, +0.009216 and +0.020155, so the benefit was uneven across replicas. Four task means increased; sitagliptin decreased. The final fifteen updates are excluded from the selection-to-proposal conclusions because no later proposals follow them.

molecular_assessment.headline: Conventional aromatic medicinal chemistry spans many cores, with concentrated high-score families and no assigned stereochemistry
molecular_assessment.overall_character: The supplied trajectories cover all five objectives and all three seeds: each task contains 900 evaluated molecules, including 870 optimizer proposals. All 4,350 optimizer-proposal SMILES parse with RDKit. This is predominantly recognizable medicinal chemistry: aromatic and heteroaromatic rings linked through amides, ureas, hydrazones, amines and sulfonamides. Proposal median heavy-atom counts are 24, 30, 28, 23 and 24 in the supplied task order; median ring counts are three throughout. Digest aromatic-token rates are 0.9586-0.9908 and ring-closure rates 0.9782-0.9977, so lack of rings or aromaticity is not the central deficit. Across individual tasks, 392-737 distinct nonchiral Murcko scaffolds occur among proposals, although the digest leaders repeatedly occupy close analogue families. Dominant structures have plausible conventional connectivity; occasional azides, peroxides, haloalkyl chains and very large products warrant separate scrutiny. These trajectories do not establish synthesis, stability, solubility or experimental activity. Relative to the parent, aromatic medicinal chemistry remains central, while the leading families change: pyrazole carboxamides and pyrrolylmethyl ureas replace prominent indole amides, flexible diamines join the strongest amine chemotypes, and acylhydrazones are more prominent in one otherwise weak-score session. No assigned stereocentres occur in optimizer proposals; molecules with unassigned stereocentres number 107, 76, 338, 201 and 286 in task order. Ring-rich generation therefore coexists with incomplete stereochemical specification.

per_task.generated_character: Proposals usually have a compact aromatic framework: median 24 heavy atoms and three aromatic rings. The leading approximately 0.470 family consists of N-aryl pyrazole carboxamides bearing an N-(1-arylethyl) amide substituent; the approximately 0.468 family comprises an N-methylpyrrolylmethyl group attached to a diaryl urea. Both are conventional three-ring medicinal-chemistry structures with carbonyl hydrogen-bonding groups and substantial aryl halogenation. An aza-fused aromatic hydroxy carboxamide also appears among the digest leaders. This differs from the parent leaders, which included substituted indole carboxamides. The low end includes long-chain ester elaboration and much larger, multiply linked ring systems, rather than an absence of valid or aromatic structures.
liabilities: Repeated aryl bromine and chlorine substitution can increase molecular mass without demonstrating a score benefit in the cited equal-score families.
Long alkyl tails and elaborate linked frameworks produce severe low-score outliers despite chemically recognizable bonding.
missing_features: Systematic exploration of alternative compact aromatic/carbonyl arrangements is underrepresented among the leading examples relative to repeated halogen variants; no specific unobserved target scaffold can be inferred.
The leading arylethyl carboxamides contain an unassigned stereogenic carbon, so the generated molecules do not specify which three-dimensional configuration is being proposed.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The supplied leaders associate moderate molecular size and organized aromatic/carbonyl substitution with scores near 0.47. Scores are identical within several halogen substitutions and positional variants, so these examples do not establish a reward for further halo decoration. Extending an indole ester with a very long alkyl chain gives about 3.14e-24, while an elaborate ring-and-linker-rich amide reaches about 9.07e-27. Those comparisons support size and arrangement sensitivity, but are not matched transformations isolating a single cause. Final pyrrolylmethyl urea analogues score about 0.423-0.436, showing that related heteroaromatic substitutions can retain appreciable score without reaching the listed maximum.

per_task.generated_character: This is the largest and most halogen-rich typical proposal set: median 30 heavy atoms, median molecular mass 437.343 and digest halogen rate 0.8701. The leading molecules have three aromatic six-membered rings, heavily fluorinated aryl groups, a substituted pyridine core, and aminomethyl, benzylamine or amide connections. A separate leading family contains diarylamino acylhydrazones. These are plausible synthetic motifs, although their dense fluorination and largely aromatic frameworks create substantial mass and polarity-distribution questions. Full trajectories contain 187 proposals matching an N-N=C connection. Compared with the parent, fluorinated aromatic and hydrazone chemistry persists, with the current leaders including less fused, three-ring pyridyl amine and amide architectures.
liabilities: Dense aryl fluorination and mostly aromatic frameworks can produce high molecular mass and limited three-dimensional shape; the trajectories contain no physical-property measurements.
Acylhydrazones and thiourea/imine variants introduce geometry, tautomerism and stability questions that a valid SMILES string does not settle.
Nine optimizer proposals exceed 50 heavy atoms; extending size is not itself supported as the useful structural feature.
missing_features: The leading repertoire supplies many fluorinated aromatic analogues but less evidence for chemically different architectures retaining the same useful spatial and electronic arrangement.
Hydrazone and imine examples do not specify C=N geometry; their displayed scores do not identify which configurational or tautomeric form would carry the implied interactions.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The top aminomethyl pyridyl structure scores 0.603953 and related amines or amides lie close to 0.60. A useful local contrast is the methylthio pyridyl amide at 0.599304 versus its methylsulfonyl counterpart at 0.343569: the rest of their displayed framework is the same, supporting sensitivity to sulfur oxidation state in that chemical context. It does not establish that sulfones are generally unfavorable. The small cyanophenyl sulfone scores 0.257003, whereas terminal aromatic thiourea/imine structures reach approximately 0.57-0.59. Size alone therefore does not explain the full gradient.

per_task.generated_character: The strongest displayed chemistry includes very flexible acyclic diamines: a tertiary nitrogen connects an N-butyl group, an arylbutyl group and a propyl secondary-benzylamine arm. Those molecules carry two halogenated aromatic rings and no saturated nitrogen ring. Another high-scoring family combines an arylpiperidine with an aminoethyl arylamine substituent. These are recognizable amine-rich medicinal-chemistry structures, with median proposal heavy-atom count 28 and median fraction of sp3 carbons about 0.529. Parent leaders instead prominently included arylpiperazine/indole combinations and fused aryl amines, so useful amine-plus-aromatic chemistry spans several topologies. Low-score examples are often amide-, sulfonamide- or acylhydrazone-rich aromatic structures with fewer clearly basic aliphatic amine sites.
liabilities: Long alkyl linkers, N-butyl or N-pentyl groups and heavy aryl halogens create substantial conformational freedom and mass; the leading chlorobromo diamine has molecular mass 465.907.
Several cited terminal molecules carry primary bromoalkyl or iodoalkyl groups, introducing possible electrophilic side-chain liabilities that the objective values do not characterize.
Ten proposals exceed 50 heavy atoms and the largest reaches 81, so the proposal distribution includes much larger structures than the leading compact ring/amine frameworks.
missing_features: No additional functional group can be inferred as necessary from near-ceiling scores; broader economical coverage of the observed amine/aromatic arrangements is the supported chemical coverage gap.
Three-dimensional specification remains incomplete across the full proposal set: 338 proposals contain an unassigned stereocentre, although the leading flexible diamine itself is achiral.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The flexible diamines reach 0.999998 and the arylpiperidine example 0.999994. Both retain accessible amine functionality and separated aromatic regions, supporting those shared features as a chemical association in this trajectory; a saturated nitrogen ring is not required by the leading examples. A compact nitro/acid heteroaromatic amide is near 1.86e-05 and a sulfonamide-substituted heteroaryl amide near 1.98e-05. In the final molecules, a tertiary amine with two bromobutyl arms and no aromatic ring scores 0.123770, while more extended molecules retaining a benzylamine-bearing aryl region score around 0.90 or above. These are contextual associations rather than measured binding or isolated substituent effects.

per_task.generated_character: Median proposals contain 23 heavy atoms and three rings, with 729 distinct nonchiral Murcko scaffolds among optimizer proposals. The leading family is arylsulfonylpiperazine chemistry: examples attach sulfonyl phenylpiperazine to a fused aza-lactam or chromanone-like framework, or attach N-methylpiperazine sulfonamide to substituted biphenyl systems. Those molecules combine aromatic surfaces, a saturated six-membered nitrogen ring, sulfonyl oxygens and sometimes an additional carbonyl. The parent also produced a leading N-methyl arylsulfonylpiperazine, alongside fused lactam and diaryl heterocyclic alternatives. The current leading structures are generally plausible synthetic chemotypes; the very low end includes carbon disulfide, allyl azide and small unusual or highly polar fragments.
liabilities: Small disconnected-from-the-leading-chemotype proposals include carbon disulfide and an organic azide, yielding little useful structural overlap with the higher-scoring multi-ring molecules.
Sulfonylation changes the electronic character of a ring nitrogen; counting every nitrogen as an interchangeable basic amine would misdescribe this family.
Some terminal proposals add multiple sulfur/nitrogen connections and tautomeric heterocycles without demonstrating improved placement of the leading polar groups.
missing_features: The output covers many core identities but supplies limited evidence for precise alternative placements of its useful aromatic, sulfonyl and amine regions beyond the leading analogue neighborhood.
Leading alternatives include an unspecified stereocentre in the chromanone-like example, and 201 proposals have an unassigned stereocentre; configurationally explicit versions are absent.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The fused aza-lactam sulfonylphenylpiperazine reaches 0.235468, a chromanone-like analogue 0.229568 and a methoxy biphenyl N-methylsulfonylpiperazine 0.222204. These support a combined multi-ring and polar-linker architecture in the observed neighborhood. Carbon disulfide and allyl azide score zero, while a heavily hydroxylated cyclic acid scores 0.013472: fragmentation or abundant oxygen alone does not reproduce the arrangement in the leaders. Other aromatic, carbonyl-containing terminal molecules remain near 0.10-0.15. The molecular evidence does not identify a single missing substituent capable of resolving the remaining low scores.

per_task.generated_character: The highest molecule is a compact N-methylbenzamide attached to a substituted fused azaheteroaromatic system bearing a hydroxyl group; it has 22 heavy atoms and three aromatic rings. Other leaders are substituted anisyl/pyridyl acylhydrazones, generally with two aromatic rings, and an aryl hydroxyethyl carboxamide attached to a pyrazole. These are recognizable, synthetically plausible chemical families rather than unusual-valence graphs. Full proposals have median 24 heavy atoms, three rings and 737 distinct nonchiral Murcko scaffolds. Relative to the parent leaders, which included sulfonamide/acyl heterocycles and fused imino carbonyl systems, the current digest is particularly concentrated in pyridyl acylhydrazones; N-N=C matches increase from 71 to 116 proposals. Worst examples include extremely large polycyclic, macrocyclic peptide-like or long-chain aromatic elaborations.
liabilities: Acylhydrazone enrichment brings possible E/Z, tautomeric and stability concerns that are not resolved by the objective scores.
Large aromatic appendages, long alkyl chains and oversized cyclic structures coincide with vanishing scores; six proposals exceed 50 heavy atoms.
The proposal set contains 286 molecules with an unassigned stereocentre and no assigned stereocentres, limiting interpretation of any geometry-dependent chemistry.
missing_features: Broader coverage of compact, correctly arranged polar heteroaromatic/carbonyl chemotypes is missing from the higher-score repertoire, which repeatedly returns close acylhydrazone analogues despite many proposed scaffolds.
The hydroxyethyl amide leader has an unassigned stereogenic alcohol carbon, while hydrazone leaders do not specify C=N geometry; these structures do not establish stereochemical adequacy.

The evidence supports no unique mandatory target-like group: the best displayed molecule is distinct from the repeated hydrazone family, so extrapolation should preserve access to alternative compact cores.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The compact benzamide/azaheteroaromatic structure scores 0.309504, the acetyl-substituted anisyl pyridyl acylhydrazone 0.281351, and the hydroxyethyl pyrazole carboxamide 0.274759. A dimethoxy aryl pyridyl acylhydrazone scores 0.233893, whereas the corresponding displayed acetyl hydrazone with the heteroaryl acyl region replaced scores 0.002010. Enlarging a methoxy substituent to a benzyl/CF3-bearing arm gives approximately 1.33e-09 despite retaining a pyridyl acylhydrazone. Thus functional-group placement and controlled size both appear relevant within the visible examples. The digest median is rounded to 0.0: the full 900-row trajectory median is approximately 3.19e-07 and only two rows are exactly zero. The displayed higher-score chemotypes occupy a sparse part of a mostly very low-score distribution.

transferable_gaps.evidence: A displayed pyridyl amide scores 0.599304 with a methylthio substituent and 0.343569 with the corresponding methylsulfonyl group. In another supplied session, a pyridyl acylhydrazone scores 0.233893 while the displayed acetyl hydrazone counterpart scores 0.002010. High-scoring amine-rich structures also differ chemically from lower-scoring amide and sulfonamide nitrogen environments. These examples show that heteroatom counts alone do not explain the observed gradient.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator covers many atoms and functional groups but does not consistently preserve their useful attachment and electronic context.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Preserve access to chemically valid attachment-point and oxidation-state alternatives, and learn their value from observed feedback in their local structural context. Treat amines, amide nitrogens, sulfonamide nitrogens, thioethers and sulfones as different chemical environments rather than interchangeable token decorations.

transferable_gaps.evidence: Individual proposal sets contain 392-737 distinct nonchiral Murcko scaffolds, yet digest leaders cluster into pyrazole carboxamides, pyrrolylmethyl ureas, polyfluorinated pyridyl structures, flexible diamines, arylsulfonylpiperazines and acylhydrazones. Several halo-substitution or positional variants have identical displayed scores. Another session contains 737 scaffold identities while its full-trajectory median score is approximately 3.19e-07, showing that identity breadth is not sufficient chemical coverage of useful regions.
transferable_gaps.gap: Broad scaffold counts coexist with narrow high-score analogue families and repeated peripheral halogen variation.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Support core and linker alternatives that preserve chemically meaningful arrangements already associated with reward, alongside local substitution. Assess useful chemical coverage from observed structural neighborhoods and feedback, without assuming that more unique strings or more halogen substitutions alone expands the productive repertoire.

transferable_gaps.evidence: No assigned stereocentres occur in the 4,350 optimizer proposals; the five sessions contain 107, 76, 338, 201 and 286 proposals with at least one unassigned stereocentre. Digest leaders include an arylethyl carboxamide, a chromanone-like ring and a benzylic alcohol whose stereocentres are unspecified. Acylhydrazone leaders also omit explicit C=N geometry. The leading flexible diamine is achiral, so stereochemical specification is a conditional need rather than a universal requirement.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator leaves stereogenic structures and configurationally ambiguous imine chemistry unspecified.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Represent and sample stereochemistry where a generated structure actually supports it, retaining chemically consistent configurations and bond geometry. Let feedback determine the usefulness of these alternatives, and keep achiral and configurationally explicit structures accessible without assuming an unobserved preferred stereoisomer.

transferable_gaps.evidence: Proposal median heavy-atom counts are 24, 30, 28, 23 and 24, but the numbers exceeding 50 heavy atoms are 1, 9, 10, 0 and 6. Cited low-score molecules include very long alkyl esters and oversized aromatic or macrocyclic structures. In a close hydrazone neighborhood, replacing a compact methoxy substituent with a benzyl/CF3-bearing extension accompanies a score near 1.33e-09. Conversely, flexible multi-amine chains can score near the ceiling, while some related proposals introduce primary bromoalkyl or iodoalkyl groups.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator lacks consistent context-sensitive control of molecular growth, flexible side chains and reactive appendages.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Maintain alternatives with controlled linker length, appendage size and functional-group reactivity, using local feedback to distinguish useful flexibility from destructive growth. A single global preference for small, rigid or ring-bound structures would discard demonstrated useful chemistry; the needed capability is contextual structural control and chemically informed handling of side-chain motifs.

approach.method_basis: The Parent first trains a recurrent SMILES language model on an unlabeled molecular corpus. Each objective starts with a fresh policy copied from that prior, which then stays frozen. After each accepted batch, the policy fits the best-scoring half of the current molecules and a uniformly sampled group of earlier elites. Every target is the frozen prior log probability of the molecule's original accepted SMILES plus sixty times its real score, with equal weight for each training sequence. A memory keeps the thirty-two highest-scoring previously selected elites, preserving their original strings and scores. The updated policy directly samples complete SMILES, and chemical validation and canonical duplicate rejection fill the next batch.
approach.novelty: Replace uniform historical sampling with score-ordered replay: use the highest-scoring eligible historical molecules, keeping the same replay count. This makes the best accepted evidence already present in memory determine the historical training group. It leaves admission, retention and the learning rule intact. Earlier siblings explored the prior representation and training; the original replay experiment established that using history changes learning, but did not test whether preferentially selecting stronger history helps. A passive uniform draw on the same memory and a comparison of the two gradients will show whether this selection changes the evidence actually fitted. Concentration and useful novel molecules remain separate outcomes, because repeatedly choosing strong examples can also narrow exploration.
